Main findings: 1. Pregnant and breastfeeding women were overall accepting of PrEP and highly valued safety for mother and child regarding PrEP use. Some reported fears about miscarriage or birth defects resulting from PrEP use. They stressed the importance of personal choice in HIV pre- vention and wished to have a variety of options so they could choose the product that worked best for them. 2. Participants feared exacerbation of pregnancy symptoms such as vaginal discomfort with the DVR or nausea for oral pills. Taboos against vaginal insertion or taking medicine during pregnancy could be a barrier to initiation for both formulations. 3. Partner support was paramount, and women typically considered PrEP use to be a decision

made in conjunction with their partners. 1. Though awareness of PrEP was low, 95.8% of participants were willing to use PrEP. Men were more likely to prefer on-demand (65.2% vs. 53.8%) while women were more likely to prefer daily (46.3% vs. 34.8%). 2. Preference for on-demand was driven by dislike of daily tablets and believing one was not frequently enough at risk to justify daily dosing.
